sentences.text: Physornis is an extinct genus of flightless bird belonging to the family Phorusrhacidae, and it is considered one of the largest known terror birds.
Based on relatives, Physornis may have reached a height of 2 meters at the head, and recent studies estimate it was over 2 meters tall and similar in size to Brontornis.

The fragmentary nature of the fossils makes determining the size of Physornis difficult, though its mandible branches are further apart from the median, suggesting a wider skull base compared to Phorusrhacos.
The mandibular symphysis of Physornis is constricted, wide, and has a flat ventral side.
One preserved mandible specimen measured 15 cm in length.
Large lacrimal bone expansions above the eyes suggest it hunted by sight in open, sunlit areas rather than shaded forests.
Physornis was scientifically described by Florentino Ameghino in 1895.

Fossils of Physornis have only been found in Deseadan deposits in Santa Cruz and Chubut Provinces, with the first fossils discovered in the Pyrotherium beds near Puerto Deseado in eastern Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.
An Amherst College expedition to Argentina's Sarmiento Formation began in 1911.

Physornis shares characteristics with graviportal, large-bodied dromornithids and Gastornis, and it had a graviportal macropedatory ecological role. Unlike the running genera Phorusrhacos, Procariama, and Psilopterus, Physornis was a graviportal ambush hunter.
Physornis likely preyed on large mammals.
Physornis was flightless, evidenced by the proportional size of its wings and body mass, with wing size being more reduced in larger group members.

Dreyer and colleagues used ground-section microscopy on bone samples from the FM-P13619 limb bones to study Physornis growth. Physornis displayed a pattern of rapid growth similar to modern birds, indicated by a transition from vascularized to laminar bone tissue. Physornis fossils lacked lines of arrested growth (LAGs), indicating continuous bone growth without pauses.
Researchers suggest that cursoriality and graviportality exist on a spectrum, and Physornis may have been capable of short, fast bursts of speed.

Alvarenga and Höfling classified Physornis as a close relative of Paraphysornis and Brontornis, noting Brontornis is now a galliform. Argentine paleontologist Federico Agnolín established the subfamily Physornithinae for Physornis and Paraphysornis in 2007.
Brodkorb and other studies have considered Aucornis eurhynchus a synonym of P. fortis.
The species formerly known as P. brasiliensis is now classified in the genus Paraphysornis.

Physornis fossils date from the Oligocene to the Miocene epochs, and Physornis lived in South America during the Oligocene. The time range for Physornis is from the Rupelian to the Late Pleistocene, approximately 29 to 0.0117 million years ago.
Physornis lived during the Oligocene epoch in what is now Argentina.

In 1941, Bryan Patterson suggested the holotype might not be avian. Patterson speculated the holotype could be a fragment from a giant mammal like Parastrapotherium or Pyrotherium. Patterson provisionally classified the holotype as a nomen dubium.
There is a discrepancy in the recorded time range for Physornis, with one source citing the Oligocene while the Paleobiology Database lists a range from the Rupelian to the Late Pleistocene.
